questions.prompt: Which statement about Python versus DAX is correct, per this course?
options: DAX recalculates live per filter/click; a Python script also recalculates live when a user interacts with a visual, so either tool can be used interchangeably.
Python is faster than DAX for every calculation, so it should replace DAX whenever possible.
DAX can only be used in calculated columns, never in measures that respond to filters.
DAX recalculates live per filter/click; a Python script runs once at import or refresh and produces a static result, so DAX can't be replaced by Python.
Python and DAX solve the exact same problem, so the choice is purely a matter of personal preference.
DAX needs Python installed on the machine to run correctly.
questions.explain: DAX measures recalculate live, per visual, per filter context, every time a user clicks around a report. A Python script runs once, at import or refresh time, and produces a static result — if a calculation needs to respond to what a user clicks, that's DAX's job, with no exceptions.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A is the closest wrong answer because a Python visual genuinely can respond to filtering and highlighting from other visuals on the page — but that's the visual re-running its script once per interaction and redrawing a new static chart, not a live, continuously-recalculating formula the way a DAX measure is. That one detail — 'also recalculates live' — is the actual error.

questions.prompt: A script run through Power BI's Get Data → Python script creates a Python list, a Python dictionary, and one DataFrame named `df`. Only `df` shows up as loadable in the Navigator window. Why?
options: Power BI can only import a Pandas DataFrame — not a list or a dictionary.
The list and dictionary need to be converted with print() first.
Power BI only shows the last variable created, regardless of its type.
Lists and dictionaries need an explicit import pandas as pd line to be visible.
questions.explain: Power BI's Python data source can only import a Pandas DataFrame. A plain list or dictionary, no matter how the script uses it, never appears as a loadable table in the Navigator — only DataFrame variables do.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so this line is a valid f-string that embeds the variables directly: print(________"Total for {customer_name} is {order_total}")
questions.explain: An f-string is written by placing an f immediately before the opening quote. That's what lets {customer_name} and {order_total} be embedded directly inside the string instead of being passed as separate comma-separated arguments to print().

questions.code:
products = ["Widget A", "Widget B", "Widget C"]
products.append("Widget D")
print(products[-1])
questions.prompt: What does this print?
options: Widget D
Widget C
Widget A
An error, because -1 isn't a valid index
questions.explain: `.append()` adds "Widget D" to the end of the list, making it the last item. `-1` always means "the last item" in a Python list, regardless of the list's length, so products[-1] returns "Widget D".

questions.prompt: A script needs to store one customer's name, region, and total orders as a single labeled record, accessed by name rather than by position. Select every line below that correctly builds that kind of record.
options: customer = {"name": "Alex Rivera", "region": "West", "total_orders": 12}
customer = ["Alex Rivera", "West", 12]

customer = {"name": "Alex Rivera", "region": "West"}
customer["total_orders"] = 12
name, region, total_orders = "Alex Rivera", "West", 12
questions.explain: A dictionary is the structure that's accessed by name instead of position — options A and C both end up as the exact same dictionary, just built in one step versus two (adding the third key afterward is exactly how a dictionary is normally updated). Option B is a list, which is accessed by numeric position, not by name. Option D creates three separate variables with no shared structure linking them together as one record at all.

questions.code:
import pandas as pd
data = {"Product": ["Widget A", "Widget B"], "Units Sold": [120, 85]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df.shape)
questions.prompt: What does this print?
options: ['Product', 'Units Sold']
questions.explain: `.shape` returns (row count, column count). This DataFrame has 2 rows and 2 columns (Product, Units Sold), so it prints (2, 2).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank to complete the standard import line used at the top of nearly every script in this course: import pandas as ________
questions.explain: `import pandas as pd` is the near-universal convention for loading Pandas under the short nickname pd — so standard that seeing pd.anything() in someone else's code is instantly recognizable as Pandas.

questions.prompt: A column that should hold whole numbers shows as `object` in `.dtypes`. What does this most likely mean?
options: The column is actually storing the numbers as text (strings), not real numbers
The column contains missing values (NaN)
The DataFrame has more rows than columns
The column was never loaded into Power BI
questions.explain: object is Pandas' label for text, including numbers stored as text. A column of numbers can load as object for reasons that have nothing to do with the numbers themselves — a stray currency symbol, inconsistent formatting, or a source system that quoted every value as a string.

questions.prompt: This line raises an error when run. What's actually wrong with it?
options: Pandas needs & instead of and when combining row-wise filter conditions
The column names need to be lowercase
df["Region"] == "West" should be df["Region"] = "West"
The parentheses around each condition should be removed
questions.explain: Regular Python's and/or keywords expect a single True/False value, but each side of this comparison is actually a whole column of True/False values, one per row. Pandas needs & (and) or | (or) instead, with parentheses kept around each condition, to combine conditions row by row.

questions.prompt: A DataFrame df has duplicate Product values that need to be reduced to one row per product, keeping the first occurrence seen. Select every line below that correctly achieves this.
options: df.drop_duplicates(subset=["Product"])
df[~df["Product"].duplicated()]
df.dropna(subset=["Product"])
df.drop_duplicates()
questions.explain: Both A and B correctly keep exactly one row per unique Product. A narrows drop_duplicates() to just the Product column. B uses Product's own .duplicated() (True for repeats after the first), then keeps everything that's NOT flagged with ~. C is wrong because dropna() removes missing values, not duplicates — it does nothing about repeated products. D is wrong because drop_duplicates() with no subset compares the entire row, so two rows with the same Product but a different value in some other column would both survive — it doesn't guarantee one row per product.

questions.prompt: A column Units Sold loaded from a CSV shows as object instead of a number, and calling .sum() on it produces an unexpected result instead of a clean error. What's actually happening?
options: The values are strings that merely look like numbers, so a sum-style operation concatenates the text instead of adding the values
Pandas silently converts the text to 0 before summing
.sum() only works on a column named "Revenue"
The column contains NaN values that break the sum silently
questions.explain: Text that merely looks like a number can't be summed the way you'd expect — Pandas is treating each value as a string, and string handling concatenates characters instead of adding values, silently producing nonsense instead of an error you'd notice right away.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank to correctly convert a text date column into Pandas' real date type: df["Order Date"] = ________(df["Order Date"])
questions.explain: pd.to_datetime() converts a text column into Pandas' actual datetime64 date type. Once converted, the column supports real date operations — comparing, sorting, and calculating differences — none of which work correctly on a plain text string, no matter how date-shaped it looks.

questions.prompt: Match each Pandas method to what it actually does.
right: Removes any row containing at least one missing value
Returns True/False showing exactly where values are missing
Removes leading and trailing whitespace from text
Replaces missing values with a chosen value
questions.explain: .isna() only reports where gaps are, without changing anything. .fillna(0) replaces every NaN with the value given. .dropna() removes any row with at least one missing value entirely. .str.strip() is unrelated to missing values — it removes stray leading/trailing spaces from text.

questions.prompt: A Revenue column has some missing values. Which statement correctly describes how to think about .fillna() versus .dropna() for this column?
options: .fillna() removes rows with missing values, and .dropna() fills them with zero.
.isna() is the only method that actually changes the DataFrame; .fillna() and .dropna() just preview the result.
.dropna() removes any row with a missing value entirely, while .fillna() replaces missing values with a chosen value — and .fillna() is always the safer choice because it never deletes data.
.dropna() only works on numeric columns, and .fillna() only works on text columns.

.dropna() removes any row with a missing value entirely, while .fillna() replaces missing values with a chosen value — which one is right depends on what a missing value actually means for that column, not a fixed rule.
.fillna() and .dropna() do the same thing; the only difference is which one runs faster.
questions.explain: Neither method is universally "more correct." Use .dropna() when a missing value makes a row genuinely unusable, and .fillna() when a sensible default actually exists — the right choice depends on what the missing value means for that specific column, for example whether a missing Revenue means "zero sales" or "we don't actually know."
questions.distractorExplain: Option C gets both method definitions right, which makes it tempting — but it adds the claim that .fillna() is "always the safer choice because it never deletes data." That's the one wrong detail: filling a missing revenue with 0 when the true meaning was "unknown, not zero" actively misrepresents the data, which is exactly the judgment call the lesson says has no fixed, universal answer.

questions.code:
df["Profit"] = df["Revenue"] - df["Cost"]
df["Profit Margin %"] = ((df["Profit"] / df["Revenue"]) * 100).round(1)
questions.prompt: For a row where Revenue is 2400.0 and Cost is 1400.0, what value lands in Profit Margin % after this code runs?
This line raises an error. What's the actual mistake, and what should replace it?
options: .sum("mean", "count") isn't valid — getting multiple aggregations at once requires .agg(["sum", "mean", "count"]) instead
groupby("Region") should come after ["Revenue"], not before it
"Region" needs to be written without quotes
.sum() can't be used on a Series, only on a whole DataFrame
questions.explain: .sum() takes no arguments like this — it's a single aggregation. Getting sum, mean, and count together in one pass over the grouped data requires .agg(["sum", "mean", "count"]) instead of trying to pass extra aggregation names into .sum().

questions.prompt: A pipeline merges sales into products on Product, written as pd.merge(sales, products, on="Product", how=...). Every row from sales must survive even if a product's category is missing, but any products row for a product with no matching sales must NOT appear in the result. Which how is correct?
options: "left"
"inner"
"right"
"outer"
questions.explain: "left" keeps every row from the first (left) table — sales here — whether it finds a matching product or not, while dropping any products-only rows that have no matching sale. "inner" would wrongly drop sales rows with no matching product. "right"/"outer" would both wrongly keep products rows that have no matching sales row, which the scenario explicitly rules out.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for cleaning and combining two freshly loaded CSVs before grouping the result.
items: Check .dtypes and .shape on each to confirm they loaded correctly
Clean text columns with .str.strip() and fix inconsistent case
Merge the two tables with pd.merge() on their shared column
Group the merged result with .groupby() and aggregate
questions.explain: Load first, then sanity-check what actually loaded (Lesson 8's habit) before trusting it. Clean text values next, since an un-stripped or inconsistently-cased key column can silently break the merge that comes after it. Merge the two tables, and only then group and aggregate the combined result — grouping before the merge would mean grouping incomplete data.

questions.prompt: A script needs to run once, before the model loads, and produce an entirely new table from a source Power BI doesn't natively support. Which feature is the correct fit?
options: Get Data → Python script
Run Python Script, inside Power Query Editor's Transform tab
The Python visual
A DAX calculated column
questions.explain: Get Data → Python script makes Python the entire data source, producing a brand-new table from scratch. Run Python Script instead operates on data Power BI already loaded — it's handed an existing table automatically as the dataset variable, which doesn't fit "a source Power BI doesn't natively support" at all.

questions.prompt: A report needs a total that must update instantly whenever someone clicks a slicer on the report page. Which tool is correct, and why?
options: DAX — because it recalculates live, per filter context, which is exactly what a slicer-driven total needs
Python, via the Python visual — because Python visuals can respond to filtering from other visuals
Power Query, via a calculated column — because it runs during the query's transform step
Python, via Get Data → Python script — because it's the most powerful of the three tools
questions.explain: A total that needs to change the instant someone clicks a slicer needs to recalculate live, per filter context — that's DAX's defining job. A Python visual can redraw in response to filtering, but it does so by re-running its script and producing a new static image, not by acting as a live, reusable number other visuals and measures can build on the way a DAX measure can.
